ety.text: From Middle English madame, from Old French madame, from ma (“my”) + dame (“lady”), from post-classical Latin mea domina. Doublet of Madonna.

senses.d: A polite form of address for a woman or lady.
ex: Mrs Grey wondered if the outfit she was trying on made her look fat. The sales assistant just said, “It suits you, madam”.
Later, Mrs Grey was sitting in her favourite tea shop. “Would madam like the usual cream cakes and patisserie with her tea?” the waitress asked.

senses.d: The mistress of a household.
A conceited or quarrelsome girl.
ex: Selina kept pushing and shoving during musical chairs. The nursery school teacher said she was a bad-tempered little madam.

senses.d: A woman who runs a brothel, particularly one that specializes in finding prostitutes for rich and important clients.
ex: After she grew too old to work as a prostitute, she became a madam.

senses.d: A hated or contemptuous woman; used as a general term of abuse
To address as "madam".
ex: "I don't care," she said. "They'll be dead in a few minutes if you'll just do your job. Stop madaming me and get to work."
CAPTAIN WAZBA: (On Mrs. Nabele) Madam! / MRS NABELE: Will you stop madamming me? Madam! Madam! When did that start?

senses.d: To be a madam; to run (a brothel).
ex: Ray [Aghayan] also used warm golden colors for the friendly whorehouse madamed by Melina Mercouri.

senses.d: Insane; crazy; mentally deranged.
ex: You want to spend a thousand pounds on a pair of shoes? Are you mad?
He's got this mad idea that he's irresistible to women.

senses.d: Angry; annoyed.
ex: Are you mad at me?

senses.d: Used litotically to indicate satisfaction or approval.
ex: Wow, you really made this pie from scratch? I'm not mad at it.
I'm not mad at this little house, though.

senses.d: Bizarre; incredible.
ex: It's mad that I got that job back a day after being fired.

senses.d: Extremely foolish or unwise; irrational; imprudent.
Wildly confused or excited.
ex: to be mad with terror, lust, or hatred
It is the land of graven images, and they are mad upon their idols.

senses.d: Extremely enthusiastic about; crazy about; infatuated with; overcome with desire for.
ex: Aren't you just mad for that red dress?
My wife is soccer-mad.

senses.d: Abnormally ferocious or furious; or, rabid, affected with rabies.
ex: a mad dog

senses.d: Intensifier, signifying abundance or high quality of a thing; very, much, excellent or many.
ex:
I gotta give you mad props for scoring us those tickets.
 Their lead guitarist has mad skills.
 There are always mad girls at those parties.

senses.d: Having impaired polarity.
Intensifier; to a large degree; extremely; exceedingly; very; unbelievably.
ex: He was driving mad slow.
It's mad hot today.

senses.d: To be or become mad.
ex: The imperial Elizabetta gazed with surprise at the youthful and unpretending appearance of the little being that had set the world madding.

senses.d: To madden, to anger, to frustrate.
ex: This musick mads me, let it sound no more.
He that mads others, if he were so humoured, would be as mad himself, as much grieved and tormented […].

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French fol, from Old French fol, from Latin follem. Cognate with English fool.

Uncertain. Perhaps a Lombardic or Carolingian era borrowing from Old High German barrezzen (“to hate”) or maybe from French page (“page, serving boy”), probably via Neapolitan pazzo (compare French adage “être effronté comme un page”). Alternatively from Latin patiēns (“suffering”). Compare Sicilian pacciu.
Inherited from Latin follem (“bellows”), through the figurative sense of “airhead”. Compare French fou.

From Late Latin mattus (“drunk, intoxicated”), itself either from a contraction of a form *madĭtus (as a past participle of Latin madeō), or madidus (“drunk, tipsy”). Cognate to French mat (“matte, pale”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese louco, possibly from Andalusian Arabic لَوَق (lawaq, “stupidity”), from Arabic لاق (lāq, “to soften”). Compare Galician louco, Spanish loco and Sicilian loccu.
Unknown. Maybe from maluco (“moluccan”)- see Moluccas - or from a diminutive of malo.
From earlier doudo, of uncertain origin. Possibly a doublet of dodô /dodó.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bravo, possibly from Vulgar Latin *bravus or *brabus, from a fusion of Latin prāvus and barbarus.
Borrowed from Latin nervōsus (“sinewy; nervous”), corresponding to nervo + -oso.
